module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 218

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/218](https://www.erdosproblems.com/218)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos218

/--
The set of indices $n$ for which a prime gap is followed by a larger or equal prime gap has a
natural density of $\frac 1 2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.le : {n | primeGap n ≤ primeGap (n + 1)}.HasDensity <| 1 / 2 := by
  sorry

/--
The set of indices $n$ for which a prime gap is preceded by a larger or equal prime gap has a
natural density of $\frac 1 2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.ge : {n | primeGap (n + 1) ≤ primeGap n}.HasDensity <| 1 / 2 := by
  sorry

/--
There are infinitely many indices $n$ such that the prime gap at $n$ is equal to the prime gap
at $n+1$. This is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many arithmetic progressions of
length $3$, see `erdos_141.variants.infinite_three`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.infinite_equal_prime_gap : {n | primeGap n = primeGap (n + 1)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos218

findings.description: The docstring says the statement "is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many arithmetic progressions of length 3, see `erdos_141.variants.infinite_three`". It leaves out that the progressions must be made of three CONSECUTIVE primes. Read literally, infinitely many 3-term APs of integers (or even of primes, by van der Corput) are known to exist, so the literal equivalence claim is wrong. Under the intended reading it is correct. `consecutivePrimeArithmeticProgressions 3` consists exactly of the sets {p_a, p_{a+1}, p_{a+2}} with equal consecutive differences: `IsAPOfLength` over ℕ with `ENat.card s = 3` forces d > 0. The map a ↦ {p_a, p_{a+1}, p_{a+2}} is injective. So the Lean statement itself is unaffected; only the prose is elliptical.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/latex/218: "...(which is equivalent to $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression, see [141])". Wikipedia, Primes in arithmetic progression, section 'Consecutive primes in arithmetic progression': "unlike an AP-k, all the other numbers between the terms of the progression must be composite. For example, the AP-3 {3, 7, 11} does not qualify, because 5 is also a prime."
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to: "This is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many arithmetic progressions of three consecutive primes, see `erdos_141.variants.infinite_three`."

reformulations.difference: `primeGap n = nth Prime (n+1) - nth Prime n` uses Mathlib's 0-indexed `Nat.nth` (`nth Prime 0 = 2`). So Lean's `primeGap n` is the source's d_{n+1} (source convention p_1 = 2). The Lean set {n | primeGap n ≤ primeGap (n+1)} ⊆ ℕ is the source's set {m ≥ 1 | d_{m+1} ≥ d_m} shifted down by one. 'Density' is `Set.HasDensity`, the limit of #(S ∩ [0,b))/b.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The source set is the image of the Lean set under n ↦ n+1. For any S ⊆ ℕ, #((S+1) ∩ [0,b+1)) = #(S ∩ [0,b)), so the partial densities differ by the factor b/(b+1) → 1. Hence S has natural density α iff S+1 does. Proved in Lean without sorry (scratch file /workspace/review/shift.lean): `hasDensity_image_succ_iff` and `le_iff_source`, which is literally `{n | primeGap n ≤ primeGap (n+1)}.HasDensity (1/2) ↔ {m | 1 ≤ m ∧ d m ≤ d (m+1)}.HasDensity (1/2)` with p m := nth Prime (m-1), d m := p (m+1) - p m. Banks's phrasing #{p_n ≤ x : d_{n+1} ≥ d_n} ~ π(x)/2 is also equivalent, because π(x) takes every value in ℕ and tends to ∞.

reformulations.difference: Same 0-indexed shift as the `le` variant: the Lean set {n | primeGap (n+1) ≤ primeGap n} is the source's {m ≥ 1 | d_{m+1} ≤ d_m} shifted down by one.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Natural density is invariant under n ↦ n+1 (same lemma as above). Proved in Lean as `ge_iff_source`: `{n | primeGap (n+1) ≤ primeGap n}.HasDensity (1/2) ↔ {m | 1 ≤ m ∧ d (m+1) ≤ d m}.HasDensity (1/2)`.

reformulations.difference: Same 0-indexed shift: {n | primeGap n = primeGap (n+1)} is the source's {m ≥ 1 | d_{m+1} = d_m} shifted down by one.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An injective image preserves infinitude. Proved in Lean as `eq_iff_source`, via `Set.infinite_image_iff`.

review.notes:
The source's statement (erdosproblems.com/latex/218) is: "Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$. The set of $n$ such that $d_{n+1}\geq d_n$ has density $1/2$, and similarly for $d_{n+1}\leq d_n$. Furthermore, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $d_{n+1}=d_n$." The file's three declarations state exactly these three claims, in the right direction and with non-strict inequalities.

Checks in Lean:
- `1 / 2` elaborates as `(1 / 2 : ℝ)`, not ℕ division.
- The root `primeGap` is used, and `HasDensity` defaults to `A := Set.univ`, i.e. ordinary natural density.
- `primeGap` has no truncation or junk values because the primes are infinite. Small values check out: `primeGap 0 = 1`, `primeGap 1 = primeGap 2 = 2`, `primeGap 3 = 4`.
- None of the three statements is trivially provable or refutable.

Banks [Ba23], cited by the source, phrases the conjecture as lim N^{-1}|{n ≤ N : d_{n+1}/d_n ≥ c}| = 1/(c+1); c = 1 is exactly this index-density formulation.

Status: all three are tagged `research open`. erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (page last edited 29 Jan 2026), and teorth/erdosproblems records open. The forum only notes that sieve bounds should show equal gaps have density zero, which would make the first two parts equivalent to each other; that settles nothing. So there is no status issue.

Other observations:
- There is no `erdos_218` main declaration; all three parts of the main problem are tagged `variants`. That is a naming matter, not mathematics.
- The `ge` docstring ("a prime gap is preceded by a larger or equal prime gap") indexes by the earlier gap, which is harmless by shift invariance.
- I could not read Erdős's original [Er85c] (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1985-17.pdf): it is a scanned image with no text layer, and no OCR tool is available. The review therefore rests on the erdosproblems.com LaTeX, which a separate paraphrase in a Hugging Face dataset (attributed to Er55c) also matches.
